records.key: wms:12212:oracle integration 3 govern ai agent access with oracle integration mcp gateway
records.title: Oracle Integration 3 - Govern AI Agent Access with Oracle Integration MCP Gateway
records.rawTitle: Oracle Integration 3 - Govern AI Agent Access with Oracle Integration MCP Gateway
records.source: 28 September 2026 WMS, dashboard views, and WMS tag reports; GitHub repository/update evidence retained from 14-15 August 2026
details: Give AI agents real access to enterprise systems without losing control. Build an Oracle Integration MCP Gateway that routes, filters, and audits every tool call, and see policy enforcement in action.

AI agents that call enterprise tools need the same controls as any other system integration: known identities, least-privilege access, input validation, protected credentials, and an audit trail. Oracle Integration MCP Gateway gives MCP clients one governed endpoint in front of Oracle Integration MCP servers and approved third-party MCP servers.

In this workshop, you build a customer-support scenario end to end. You expose CRM integrations as MCP tools, register an Oracle Integration MCP server and a third-party ERP procurement server, and write AI-assisted business policies that reject malformed customer IDs. You also create tool filters that hide purchase-order approval from agents, and PII policies that mask contact data in responses. Then you combine everything in a single gateway with an ordered policy pipeline and audit tracing.

Finally, you connect an MCP client to the gateway and run prompts that succeed, span both servers, and get denied by policy. You then trace each request in Oracle Integration's Observe view.

Use Agent Factory to create an agent, connect it to live data through the Oracle MCP server, leverage Select AI for natural language data access, and build a database diagnostics agent that delivers actionable insights for real-world operations. Ready to move beyond AI demos and build agents that actually work against your enterprise data? In this 90-minute hands-on lab, you’ll go from an empty workspace to a working, deployed AI agent running on Oracle Exadata Database Service.

You’ll start by using Private Agent Factory to rapidly scaffold and configure intelligent agents, then connect them to live data through the Oracle MCP (Model Context Protocol) server the bridge that lets agents securely query, reason over, and act on data inside ExaDB. Along the way you’ll put Select AI to work, using natural language to generate SQL and converse with your data directly in the database, no external pipeline required.

To bring it all together, you’ll build a database diagnostics agent: an agent that monitors database health, investigates performance signals, and surfaces actionable insights showing how agentic AI and Oracle’s converged database combine to solve a real operational problem.

You’ll leave with hands-on experience across the full agent lifecycle build, connect, deploy and a reusable pattern you can take back and apply to your own use cases on Exadata Database Service. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

records.rawTitle: Build an AI-Powered Help Desk with Oracle APEX: From Prompt to Agent
records.source: 28 September 2026 WMS, dashboard views, and WMS tag reports; GitHub repository/update evidence retained from 14-15 August 2026
details: Build a governed AI help desk in Oracle APEX 26.1 in 90 minutes - from prompt-generated app to an AI Agent that answers from your data and acts only after you approve, free in the browser.

Build a complete AI-powered help desk application in 90 minutes with Oracle APEX — and learn the governed-AI patterns that make it enterprise-ready. You will design the data model with AI and review the SQL it proposes, generate the Horizon Help Desk application from a natural-language prompt, add plain-English analytics with AI Interactive Reports, and build a 26.1 AI Agent with declarative tools that answers from your tickets and knowledge base — and resolves a ticket only after you approve. Optional labs add AI-drafted replies and fully in-database semantic search with AI Vector Search and an ONNX embedding model.

Every AI feature comes with its governance story: token quotas you set yourself, human review of AI-generated SQL, natural language that maps to inspectable declarative settings (APEX never executes AI-generated SQL), tool allow-lists, and user-approval confirmations on write actions — plus a clear statement of what data is (and is not) sent to the model by each feature.

No OCI tenancy and no local install required: just a browser and a free Oracle account. Suitable for experienced APEX developers, Oracle Database professionals new to APEX, and
developers new to Oracle.

Learn directly from Oracle Database Product Management how to identify threats and remediate them by leveraging Oracle Database Security features. Oracle Database Security Options are an essential part of the Oracle strategy to protect data and sensitive information in Oracle Databases and offer ways to comply with recent Data Privacy regulations such as EU GDPR. In this technical workshop, participants will learn from presentations and hands-on exercises about a subset of the Oracle Database Security features and options. Learn how to build and manage a globally distributed database using Exascale’s cloud-native architecture, which delivers Exadata performance with elastic scaling, high availability, and simplified operations. Join this hands-on workshop to explore how to build and operate a globally distributed database using Oracle Globally Distributed Exadata Database on Exascale Infrastructure. This next-generation platform combines the power of sharding, built-in Raft replication, and Exascale architecture to deliver a fully managed, cloud-native database service designed for mission-critical applications.

Modern applications require global scalability, continuous availability, and low-latency access to data across regions. Traditional database architectures often struggle to meet these demands without added complexity. In this workshop, you will learn how Oracle addresses these challenges by enabling seamless data distribution across geographically dispersed environments while maintaining strong consistency and zero data loss.

Through a series of guided, hands-on labs, you will actively build, configure, and manage a distributed database environment on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). You will provision Exadata resources on Exascale Infrastructure, configure networking and security, and deploy a globally distributed database architecture. You will also work with core components such as shards and catalog databases, and perform key lifecycle operations including scaling and resource management.

This workshop highlights the advantages of Exascale Infrastructure, which decouples compute and storage to provide independent scaling, on-demand resource allocation, and consumption-based efficiency. You will experience how this architecture simplifies operations while delivering the performance, reliability, and automation expected from Exadata.

By the end of this workshop, you will have a solid understanding of how to:

- Deploy and manage a globally distributed database architecture
- Scale databases horizontally by adding and managing shards
- Configure high availability using Raft-based replication
- Monitor and manage performance across distributed environments
- Leverage OCI capabilities for secure, resilient, and scalable deployments

Whether you are a database administrator, cloud architect, or developer, this workshop will equip you with the knowledge and practical experience needed to design and operate globally distributed, enterprise-scale database systems with confidence. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Resource Analytics centralizes resource inventory across multiple tenancies and regions, offering easy access to configurations and relationships through a SQL endpoint in an Autonomous Datawarehouse . Resource Analytics synchronizes customers resource metadata into a relational data model, allowing them to query inventory in near-real time. With standardized views and seamless integration with tools like Oracle SQL Developer, accessing and analyzing inventory data has never been easier.
 
Product Features
 
Advanced troubleshooting using Graph Studio
To simplify troubleshooting, Resource Analytics uses Graph Studio, an integrated Autonomous Data Warehouse feature, to visually represent resource relationships. This intuitive graphical interface helps you quickly understand connections between resources, enabling faster issue resolution. With a right-click, you can access detailed properties or navigate directly to the resource for immediate action, making resource management and addressing issues more efficient and accessible.
 
Built-in inventory insights via OAC (Oracle Analytics Cloud)
Customers can configure Resource Analytics to provision an Oracle Analytics Cloud (OAC) instance, providing built-in dashboards and reports that offer a comprehensive view of your resource inventory. These preconfigured analytics allow you to easily analyze data by region, tenancy, and compartment. You can extend these dashboards or create custom ones to meet your specific needs and even bring in custom datasets for enriched insights. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Configure Hub-and-Spoke Routing for an Active/Active Palo Alto NGFW Deployment in OCI 12168 OCI iwan.hoogendoorn@oracle.com Workshop In Development No Repository Url 12168 Workshop In Development OCI 9/23/2026 8/31/2026 Individual author Individual No Repository Url No repository URL is present in the current WMS export. GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 12168 Workshop In Development OCI 9/23/2026 8/31/2026 Individual author Individual iwan.hoogendoorn@oracle.com Learn how to steer traffic through an Active/Active Palo Alto Networks VM-Series deployment fronted by OCI Network Load Balancers in a Hub-and-Spoke topology. This workshop covers the same nine North-South and East-West routing scenarios as the standalone workshop, with every flow routed to a Trust or Untrust NLB and designed for session symmetry across both firewalls. In an Active/Active Palo Alto Networks VM-Series deployment in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), both firewalls process traffic at the same time and neither one owns the data path. OCI route rules therefore point at a Network Load Balancer (NLB) rather than at a firewall interface: an Untrust NLB for traffic entering from the Internet side, and a Trust NLB for traffic entering from the workload side. The NLB operates at Layer 4 and preserves the original source and destination addresses, which is what makes stateful inspection on the firewalls possible in the first place.

That design buys horizontal scale, but it introduces the hardest requirement in Hub-and-Spoke firewall routing: session symmetry. A session must land on the same firewall in both directions, because neither firewall holds the other's session state. Every route rule, every NLB listener, and every backend set in this workshop is built with that constraint in mind, and each scenario ends with a validation step that proves the flow is symmetric rather than merely working.

This workshop is the Active/Active variant of the final part of the Palo Alto Networks in OCI series. The earlier parts covered deploying the two firewall instances and the Trust and Untrust NLBs that front them. This part shifts the focus to routing and end-to-end connectivity around that pair.

You will work through nine routing scenarios, each with its own use case, traffic flow, OCI route table configuration, matching PAN-OS virtual router configuration on both firewalls, and a validation step.

North-South scenarios cover a public Application Load Balancer with a WAF policy placed in front of the Untrust NLB; the firewalls placed in front of a private Application Load Balancer with destination NAT; centralized outbound Internet access for spoke workloads with source NAT; and remote user access through GlobalProtect VPN terminated behind a dedicated VPN NLB, with split-tunnel routing.

East-West scenarios cover a centralized Service Gateway in the hub with full firewall inspection of Oracle Services Network traffic; distributed Service Gateways in each spoke that bypass inspection; subnet-to-subnet traffic inside a single spoke VCN forced through the firewalls; spoke-to-spoke traffic between two VCNs routed through the firewalls; and hybrid connectivity over an IPSec VPN between the OCI region hosting the firewalls and an OCI native Dynamic Routing Gateway in another region.

Because an Active/Active deployment has no configuration synchronization, you will also learn where duplicate configuration is required on the second firewall, and how to keep the two members consistent as the topology grows. Finally, you will remove one firewall from service and confirm that the NLB health checks steer new sessions to the surviving member and that the topology continues to inspect every flow you designed it to inspect. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 11138 Workshop In Development Developers - On Premises 8/14/2025 10/31/2022 Individual author Individual matthew.mcdaniel@oracle.com NA License SE This workshop will show users how to apply data mesh to an event sourcing use case about real-time credit card fraud detection. Event sourcing is a common practice for use cases that require storing changes to domain objects. For instance, in a package shipping application, one might store changes to an object in transit i.e item has shipped, item is in delivery, item has been delivered, etc. With this, we can guarantee that changes to the domain object's state are caused by these events. This gives us traceability as we can trace the state of an object by the events associated with it. When we introduce data mesh to this architecture, we can treat these events as data products, that is, we realize the potential business value of these events and publish them to analytics tools and APIs. In this workshop, we will cover one such use case in the form of real-time transaction fraud detection. The user will be responsible for configuring a Golden Gate Stream Analytics (GGSA) pipeline and a Oracle Machine Learning (OML) (IDK if this is the extent, please advise) model to accurately transform credit card transaction events into a data product, which will then be published to Oracle Analytics Server and exposed to a lightweight microservice. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

details: Learn how to monitor, diagnose, and optimize a multicloud Oracle database fleet using OCI Database Management and Ops Insights. This hands-on lab explores fleet monitoring, SQL performance, AWR and ADDM insights, capacity planning, cost management, and dashboards through guided real-world tasks.

This hands-on lab shows how OCI Database Management and Ops Insights work together to help database administrators monitor, diagnose, and optimize a multicloud Oracle database fleet. Participants begin with fleet-level visibility and learn how to identify database health, performance, capacity, and configuration concerns across managed databases and Exadata environments.
Through guided tasks, participants use Performance Hub, SQL Monitoring, AWR Explorer, AWR Hub, ADDM Spotlight, SQL Explorer, capacity planning, Exadata capacity planning, Exadata Cost Management, and Ops Insights dashboards. The lab demonstrates how historical trends, workload analysis, automated recommendations, and resource utilization insights can be combined to identify performance bottlenecks, forecast future capacity needs, optimize costs, and prioritize corrective actions.
By completing the lab, participants gain practical experience using OCI Database Management and Ops Insights to move from fleet discovery to detailed diagnosis and strategic planning. The lab is intended for database administrators, cloud administrators, architects, and technical professionals responsible for operating and optimizing Oracle databases across on-premises, OCI, and multicloud environments.

This workshop delves into the particulars of a comprehensive range of considerations essential for developers and illustrates how Oracle provides one-of-a-kind solutions across the entire spectrum of concerns. Achieving 99.999% availability for an application requires rigorous planning, sophisticated architecture, and strict operational management. This workshop delves into the comprehensive range of considerations essential for developers and illustrates how Oracle provides one-of-a-kind solutions across the entire spectrum of concerns.
The use case focus involves particular aspects, including Oracle integrations and features, of the most popular full stack software languages and platforms like Spring Boot, .NET, and JavaScript. It explores application tier architectures, highlighting the roles of Kubernetes and microservices, and examines data and message-driven applications (including details on Kafka, TxEventQ, data models, workloads, etc.).
The workshop emphasizes the importance of idempotence and eventual consistency and maintaining transactional data integrity, exploring various protocols such as XA and sagas/LRA (including MicroTx , Oracle Sagas, reservation less locking, auto-compensating data types, etc.). 
It also addresses the significance of caching and application continuity features for enhancing performance and reliability.
The course covers the use of globally distributed databases and sharding techniques to ensure scalability and availability. It outlines the critical need for compliance with regulations and underscores the details of robust security measures.
Additionally, the workshop delves into lower-level aspects like cross site recovery, Oracle DataGuard, GoldenGate, etc. providing a holistic view of the technologies and practices necessary to build highly reliable systems. 
Finally, observability, and Oracle’s end-to-end unified observability approach across all products is discussed in detail providing the ability to monitor application for failures and performance.
This comprehensive approach is designed to equip developers with the knowledge and skills required to design and operate applications that meet the demanding uptime goal of 99.999% availability, ensuring minimal downtime and maximum reliability in a variety of operating environments. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

You’ll deploy AI DB Private Agent Factory, connect it to 19c, and learn how to create data analysis agents on sample APEX data. In this hands-on learning workshop, you will learn how to build and orchestrate AI agents for legacy database environments using Oracle Database 19c and AI DB Private Agent Factory. Many enterprise workloads still run on established database versions, and this session is designed to help you apply modern agent-based patterns while keeping data access controlled and aligned with typical enterprise security expectations.

You will start by provisioning an Oracle Database 19c instance using Oracle Database Cloud Service (DBCS) to simulate an on-premises deployment. Once the database is available, you’ll install and configure Oracle REST Data Services (ORDS) and Oracle APEX to enable API access and load sample APEX data.

Next, you’ll provision AI DB Private Agent Factory and walk through the key configuration steps required to connect it to your Oracle 19c environment. With the connection in place, you’ll create data analysis agents that can work with the sample APEX data, focusing on how agents retrieve context, interpret requests, and produce reliable outputs.

Finally, you’ll design and build a custom flow that orchestrates multiple agents into an end-to-end experience—such as analyzing data, generating summaries, and guiding follow-on actions—so you leave with a repeatable blueprint you can adapt to your own legacy database use cases. By the end of the workshop, you’ll have a working reference implementation and a clear understanding of the steps, components, and best practices needed to operationalize AI agents with legacy database technologies like Oracle 19c. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 12036 Workshop Approved Analytics 5/15/2026 3/27/2026 Individual author Individual jadd.jennings@oracle.com NA Cloud SE Learn how to design and implement a simple yet expandable collaborative AI agent solution for end-to-end sales order automation using Wayflow libraries, the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, and the AI Data Platform workbench. The primary agent processes the order, delegates an availability check to a second agent through the AI Data Platform, and then sends a friendly email with the resulting report Design and implement a simple yet expandable collaborative AI agent solution that automates the sales order lifecycle end to end using Wayflow libraries, the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, and the AI Data Platform. In this solution, a primary “Order Agent” serves as the workflow owner. It ingests an incoming sales order (in this example, an object storage bucket but can also be from a chatbot, email, a web form, or an API), extracts key details such as customer, items, quantities, requested dates, and shipping preferences, and validates that the order is complete and well-formed. The Order Agent then uses the A2A protocol to delegate specialized tasks to other agents—starting with an “Inventory Agent” that checks inventory and fulfillment feasibility through the AI Data Platform. The Inventory Agent returns a structured response, enabling the Order Agent to make a clear decision or request additional information if needed.
Once availability is confirmed (or alternatives are identified), the Order Agent compiles a concise order status report and triggers an email notification to the appropriate stakeholders. The message can include key availability results, expected ship dates, backorder details, and any follow-up questions—ensuring fast, consistent communication and reducing manual effort for sales and operations teams.
The architecture is intentionally modular: each agent has a well-defined responsibility and communicates via A2A using standardized message formats. This makes the solution easy to expand beyond the initial MVP. In addition, the order agent runs as a cloud function while the inventory agent operates as a container instance. Wayflow orchestration supports reliable execution, branching, retries, and observability, while the AI Data Platform provides governed access to enterprise data for accurate, compliant decisions. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

If you are a researcher who wants to quickly deploy a GPU cluster in the cloud to run ESMFold, one of the newest and hottest machine learning (ML) applications, this is the workshop for you.

ESMFold has drawn tremendous attention since its release in July 2022 because its break-through ML model can accurately predict protein structure orders of magnitude faster than other applications.   This workshop will guide you to deploy a GPU cluster in the cloud. Then, you will move on to install and run ESMFold to predict protein structures for a dozen synthetic protein sequences.  As a bonus benefit, you will experiment with cluster autoscaling, seeing how the cluster dynamically launched and terminated nodes to meet the need of ESMFold analysis workload. 

Step-by-step instructions will be provided so you do not need previous cloud computing experience. Neither you need previous experience in ESMFold or machine learning.

Objective
In this workshop you will learn the basics of a GPU cluster architecture with Slurm managed autoscaling capability.  Then, you will work on the 4 labs in the workshop
•	Lab 1: Creating a GPU cluster to run ESMFold 
•	Lab 2: Downloading and install ESMFold software packages 
•	Lab 3: Downloading example data sets and OCI utility scripts
•	Lab 4: Executing ESMFold 

Prerequisites
•	A customer account, Oracle Paid or LiveLabs Cloud Account with service limit approved for at least 8 gpu4-count.

In this workshop you will learn to deploy OCI Streaming with Apache Kafka clusters through CLI and console. OCI Streaming with Apache Kafka is a fully managed Kafka service which allows you to build real-time, distributed data streaming pipelines, which can, collect, process, store and move millions of events per minute in a cost-efficient manner. 
You can use OCI Streaming with Apache Kafka for:
Real-time AI Training Data Foundation: Stream and aggregate real-time data from diverse sources, providing up-to-date, high-quality datasets essential for training and retraining AI and large language models (LLMs) on fresh business or operational signals.
Vector Database Pipelines for GenAI and RAG: Stream processed data, including vector embeddings, directly to integrated vector databases (such as those used in AI search or Retrieval-Augmented Generation scenarios), enabling AI models to leverage contextual and up-to-date information to enhance output relevance and accuracy.
AI Agent and Multi-Agent System Orchestration: Establish real-time communication and event sharing between AI microservices or agents, support agent state management, and coordinate dynamic workflows with streaming pipelines for more responsive and autonomous AI solutions.
Realtime Data Analysis: Continuously stream IoT and patient device data for proactive health monitoring, predictive analysis, and timely intervention.
User Behavior Analytics: Capture and process real-time data on user interactions across web and mobile applications to gain actionable insights and  personalized recommendations. 
Demand Forecasting: Stream and analyze live sales and operational data to improve on-the-fly predictions, forecasting accuracy and support data-driven business decisions.
Fraud Detection: Continuously monitor financial transactions in real time to identify suspicious patterns, anomaly detection and respond swiftly to potential fraud threats.
Change Data Capture (CDC): Seamlessly stream database changes into analytics platforms or data lakes to keep downstream systems synchronized with the latest data with low latency.
In this workshop, you will learn: 
How to create a cluster from console and OCI CLI
How to create, update and delete topics and partitions through Kafka CLI
Publishing and consuming  messages to the topics using Kafka CLI not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Vector Database Pipelines for GenAI and RAG: Stream processed data, including vector embeddings, directly to integrated vector databases (such as those used in AI search or Retrieval-Augmented Generation scenarios), enabling AI models to leverage contextual and up-to-date information to enhance output relevance and accuracy.
AI Agent and Multi-Agent System Orchestration: Establish real-time communication and event sharing between AI microservices or agents, support agent state management, and coordinate dynamic workflows with streaming pipelines for more responsive and autonomous AI solutions.
Realtime Data Analysis: Continuously stream IoT and patient device data for proactive health monitoring, predictive analysis, and timely intervention.
User Behavior Analytics: Capture and process real-time data on user interactions across web and mobile applications to gain actionable insights and  personalized recommendations. 
Demand Forecasting: Stream and analyze live sales and operational data to improve on-the-fly predictions, forecasting accuracy and support data-driven business decisions.
Fraud Detection: Continuously monitor financial transactions in real time to identify suspicious patterns, anomaly detection and respond swiftly to potential fraud threats.
Change Data Capture (CDC): Seamlessly stream database changes into analytics platforms or data lakes to keep downstream systems synchronized with the latest data with low latency.

How to create a cluster from console and OCI CLI

It returns the control and administration of the identity back to the user with the verifiable assurance based on blockchain protocols and enables users to make verifiable assertions about their identity attributes (claims). This lab will guide the user in implementing Decentralized Id (DIDs) using OBP smart contracts. Centralized approaches to managing identity data — common in today’s market — struggle to provide benefits in the three key areas: Privacy, assurance and pseudonymity. A decentralized approach uses blockchain technology to help ensure privacy, enabling individuals to validate information requests by providing the requestor with only the absolute minimum required amount of information. These are important in the emerging web3 world and Metaverse-linked applications, but DIDs are also starting to permeate into web2 enterprise applications, in areas ranging from finance to supply chain, education, healthcare, etc.

This lab will guide the user in implementing Decentralized Id (DIDs) using OBP smart contracts.  It takes a common use case in Higher Ed - a diploma certification for a graduating student and models decentralized identity process and verified claims related to student's degree awarded by a university.  The lab shows the developer how to model the data to be linked to the DIDs and how to generate the chaincodes in Blockchain App Builder for DID lifecycle leveraging some standard libraries. Once deployed, it then allows users to interact with the DIDs using the lifecycle APIs to create, share, verify DIDs and linked DID Documents.  Then a sample UI app modeling user's wallet will be set up. It will show how individual students can manage their own profile and control data sharing. And how other users acting as issuers (e.g., University administrators) will be able to provide verification of credentials. 

Based on the learning from this lab, developers will be able to implement a similar set of capabilities for many other use cases, e.g., self-sovereign health ID for sharing access to electronic health records, truck driver's credentials shared in a freight transportation marketplace, inspector's credentials in food supply chain, machinists credentials in a manufacturing space and many others. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

In this workshop, we’ll dive into MySQL’s JSON Relational Duality Views, a practical way to work with both models at once. You’ll get hands-on experience mapping complex data to clean, easy-to-use JSON structures and see how this approach can simplify your applications. Today’s developers are often caught between two worlds: they need the structure and security of relational databases, but also want the flexibility and speed that comes with JSON. MySQL’s JSON Relational Duality Views are designed to bridge that gap. This feature makes it much easier to work with modern data formats, letting teams query and update JSON documents that directly reflect what’s stored in normalized tables.

In this session, we’ll work through examples so you can see how JSON Duality Views can fit into your own projects. We’ll cover the basics what the feature is and when you’d want to use it before moving on to practical tasks like inserting, updating, and deleting data. This feature makes it much easier to work with modern data formats, letting teams query and update JSON documents that directly reflect what’s stored in normalized tables.

In this session, we’ll work through examples so you can see how JSON Duality Views can fit into your own projects. We’ll cover the basics what the feature is and when you’d want to use it before moving on to practical tasks like inserting, updating, and deleting data. You’ll also learn how concurrency control works in this context, helping you keep data reliable even as your application scales.

GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 12039 Workshop In Development Developers - Database 3/6/2026 3/6/2026 Individual author Individual eli.schilling@oracle.com NA Cloud SE In this workshop, you'll learn how to engineer memory systems that give AI agents the ability to remember, learn, and adapt across conversations. Moving beyond simple RAG, we implement a complete Memory Manager with six distinct memory types—each serving a specific cognitive function. Without engineered context, AI systems can suffer from context poisoning (repeatedly referencing a hallucination) or context distraction (irrelevant data confusing the model's logic). Proper engineering transforms a reactive chatbot into a proactive, reliable collaborator that understands project-wide dependencies.

Memory context engineering is the structured discipline of designing systems that dynamically manage what an AI model "sees" and "remembers" to ensure reliable, personalized, and efficient performance. It represents a shift from prompt engineering (crafting a single message) to system design (managing the entire lifecycle of data entering and exiting the context window).

Modern context engineering often categorizes AI memory into layers inspired by human cognitive architecture:

Short-Term Memory (Session Memory): Maintains the current conversation thread. It acts as a "scratchpad" for the AI to track its reasoning and intermediate steps during a single task.
Long-Term Memory: Persists across different sessions. This stores durable facts (e.g., "the user prefers Python") and episodic events (e.g., "the last deployment failed due to a specific flag").
Semantic vs. Episodic:
Semantic Memory: Durable, general facts and procedures.
Episodic Memory: Recalling specific past interactions or events to maintain continuity. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

details: Build an AI Lakehouse with Oracle Autonomous AI Database

Autonomous AI Lakehouse unifies data stored locally and in cloud data lakes across CSV, Parquet, JSON, ORC, Avro, and emerging table formats such as Iceberg and Delta Share. It accesses metadata managed locally through PL/SQL,AI Lakehouse delivers high-performance external-data queries at scale and supports SQL, Python, R, and REST. In this workshop, you set up an Autonomous AI Lakehouse environment and required Oracle AI Database@Azure resources, including a compartment and Azure Blob Storage. You then define external-data metadata using PL/SQL, Database Actions, or Oracle AI Database@Azure Data Catalog. Finally, you query and join lake and Azure Blob Storage data with SQL, export datasets to Azure Blob Storage, and use SQL Worksheet to explore the results.

This melding of powerful cloud infrastructure with cutting-edge AI creates a potent tool ready to revolutionize how businesses, developers, and users interact online.

5. Making Bots Alive:
Participants will then be walked through deploying their bots, integrating them with popular platforms like Slack, and ensuring the necessary security configurations are in place. Our bot, now hosted on OCI, will be capable of understanding and responding to prompts, providing intelligent and context-aware interactions.

6. Exploring the Real World:
To cap off our journey, participants will learn how to utilize their bot in real-world scenarios. Whether it's answering customer queries, providing tech support, or engaging users in meaningful conversations, the possibilities are endless. Various test scenarios will provide participants a clear understanding of how their bot behaves and how to refine its responses further.

7. Conclusion and Future Possibilities:
As we wrap up, we'll reflect on the accomplishments and the road ahead. The integration of Oracle Cloud and GPT-3 is just the beginning. The evolving landscape of AI promises even more advanced tools, and with cloud infrastructures like OCI, scaling and deploying them becomes a breeze.

records.title: Configure Hub-and-Spoke Routing for a Standalone Palo Alto NGFW Deployment in OCI
records.rawTitle: Configure Hub-and-Spoke Routing for a Standalone Palo Alto NGFW Deployment in OCI
records.source: 28 September 2026 WMS, dashboard views, and WMS tag reports; GitHub repository/update evidence retained from 14-15 August 2026
details: Learn how to steer traffic through a standalone Palo Alto Networks VM-Series firewall in an OCI Hub-and-Spoke topology. It covers nine North-South and East-West routing scenarios: public application access with a Load Balancer, central outbound Internet access with NAT, GlobalProtect remote access, Service Gateway placement, intra-VCN and spoke-to-spoke inspection, and hybrid IPSec VPN.

In a real Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) environment, a Palo Alto Networks VM-Series firewall rarely sits alone. It is deployed into a Hub-and-Spoke topology where the workloads live in spoke VCNs and the firewall sits in the hub, inspecting every flow that crosses a VCN, subnet, or zone boundary. Getting that design right is a routing problem more than a security one: get the routes right and the firewall sees every packet you want it to see, get them wrong and traffic either bypasses the firewall entirely or never reaches its destination at all.

This workshop is the final part of the Palo Alto Networks in OCI series. The earlier parts focused on deploying and configuring the firewall itself. This part shifts the focus to routing and end-to-end connectivity around a standalone (single instance) firewall deployment.

You will work through nine routing scenarios, each with its own use case, traffic flow, OCI route table configuration, matching PAN-OS virtual router configuration, and a validation step:

North-South scenarios cover a public Application Load Balancer with a WAF policy placed in front of the firewall; the firewall placed in front of a private Application Load Balancer with destination NAT; centralized outbound Internet access for spoke workloads with source NAT; and remote user access through GlobalProtect VPN with split-tunnel routing.

East-West scenarios cover a centralized Service Gateway in the hub with full firewall inspection of Oracle Services Network traffic; distributed Service Gateways in each spoke that bypass inspection; subnet-to-subnet traffic inside a single spoke VCN forced through the firewall; spoke-to-spoke traffic between two VCNs routed through the firewall; and hybrid connectivity over an IPSec VPN between the firewall in one OCI region and an OCI native Dynamic Routing Gateway in another.

Along the way you will apply the Hub-and-Spoke design guidelines that make these topologies predictable and debuggable: a dedicated hub VCN for shared services, one subnet per firewall interface, per-spoke DRG attachments with DRG route tables, DRG import route distributions so the hub learns spoke CIDRs dynamically, and DRG attachment ingress route tables that keep return traffic symmetric instead of short-circuiting back and breaking the connection.

The workshop uses specific routes in the spokes rather than a blanket default route to the hub, so that every flow you build is explicit and traceable. The centralized-egress alternative (0.0.0.0/0 to the hub) is explained where it applies, so you can choose the model that fits your production environment.

Although this workshop targets the standalone deployment, the same routing patterns apply to the Active/Passive and Active/Active deployments covered in the companion workshops. Only the route target changes.

Oracle Transactional Event Queues (TxEventQ) is a messaging platform built into Oracle Database that combines the best features of messaging and pub/sub systems. TxEventQ was introduced as a rebranding of AQ Sharded Queues in Oracle Database 21c, evolving from the Advanced Queuing (AQ) technology that has been part of Oracle Database since version 8.0. TxEventQ continues to evolve in Oracle Database 23ai, with Kafka Java APIs, Oracle REST Data Services (ORDS) integration, and many more features and integrations.

TxEventQ is designed for high-throughput, reliable messaging in event-driven microservices and workflow applications. It supports multiple publishers and consumers, exactly-once message delivery, and robust event streaming capabilities. On an 8-node Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) database, TxEventQ can handle approximately 1 million messages per second, demonstrating its scalability. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

details: Build an enterprise AI assistant that connects Microsoft Foundry agents to live data in Oracle AI Database@Azure using Oracle’s managed MCP Server. Configure secure, governed database access with Oracle MCP, then connect the MCP Server as a tool for an existing Microsoft Foundry agent.

Build an enterprise AI assistant that connects Microsoft Foundry agents to live, governed data in Oracle AI Database@Azure using Oracle’s managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.

In this hands-on workshop, you’ll learn how OCI Database Tools MCP Server provides a managed interface between AI agents and Oracle AI Database@Azure. You’ll configure an MCP Server backed by a Database Tools Connection, explore how OCI IAM Identity Domains, application roles, IAM policies, and resource principals secure access, and configure MCP toolsets that define the Oracle Database capabilities available to authorized agents.

After configuring the Oracle MCP Server, you’ll connect it to an existing agent in Microsoft Foundry. You’ll configure the required OAuth connection, make the Oracle MCP capabilities available as agent tools, and test natural-language requests that use live information from Oracle AI Database@Azure.

The workshop demonstrates how Microsoft Foundry and Oracle AI Database@Azure can work together through MCP without requiring the agent to connect directly to the database. Oracle MCP provides the managed and governed database access layer, while existing Oracle Database privileges and security controls continue to determine what data and operations are available.

By the end of the workshop, you’ll understand how to use Oracle MCP to securely connect enterprise AI agents in Microsoft Foundry with Oracle AI Database@Azure and enable agentic applications to work with trusted enterprise data.

GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 11858 Workshop In Development Database - Spatial and Graph 3/31/2025 3/22/2025 Individual author Individual maryam.sajjadian@oracle.com EMEA Sales R2RML in converged databases facilitates seamless information exchange by converting diverse data types into a unified RDF format. Converged databases handle heterogeneous data types such as JSON, XML, and CSV, which have different structures and often belong to separate domains or come from various sources. These data types do not naturally connect. However, the R2RML (RDB to RDF Mapping Language) engine provides a solution by transforming these diverse data types into a unified and interconnected RDF(Resource Description Framework) graph format.

This semantic layer helps define complex relationships between data, preserving the unique features of each source while connecting them in a flexible manner. It is referred to as a semantic layer because it adds meaning to the raw data by establishing relationships and context between different data types. Through this process, R2RML enables a better understanding and utilization of data across different domains, without the extra effort required to link data together through the various join functionalities typically used in traditional relational databases.

While traditional relational databases struggle with RDF support, applications like Spatial Studio can leverage APIs or views to access and visualize this unified RDF graph. By exposing RDF data through APIs or materialized views, even non-RDF users can seamlessly interact with and benefit from enriched spatial relationships. This approach enables applications that do not natively support RDF to still consume and utilize the data, making it more accessible for spatial analysis and visualization without requiring expertise in semantic technologies. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Building a Modular OCI Landing Zone with Modules 11991 OCI kc.flynn@oracle.com Workshop Approved No Repository Url 11991 Workshop Approved OCI 12/4/2025 1/31/2026 Individual author Individual No Repository Url No repository URL is present in the current WMS export. GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 11991 Workshop Approved OCI 12/4/2025 1/31/2026 Individual author Individual kc.flynn@oracle.com NA Cloud SE Learn how to assemble a small, non-production OCI Landing Zone using individual Core Landing Zone modules. You’ll discover where to get the modules, select a subset, configure variables via JSON, and read module outputs to supply required inputs for later modules—all from the Terraform/OpenTofu CLI. This intermediate, hands-on lab teaches you how to build a partial, non-production OCI Landing Zone using individual Core Landing Zone modules from the command line. Instead of deploying the monolithic Core Landing Zone or using the Landing Zone Orchestrator, you will work directly with a targeted subset of modules—IAM, Networking, and Tagging—to understand how the building blocks fit together and how to configure them reliably with JSON variable files and version pins. 

You will learn where to obtain the official modules, how to select only those required for a small-scale environment, and how to structure a simple, repeatable workspace for Terraform or OpenTofu. After each module apply, you will read the module’s outputs (for example, compartment OCIDs, VCN and subnet OCIDs, and tag namespace OCIDs) and manually use those values as inputs when configuring subsequent modules. This deliberate, manual handoff is designed to build confidence in interpreting outputs and understanding module boundaries before you progress to orchestration. 

The lab emphasizes practical, day-to-day skills: 

    Discover and pin module versions for reproducibility.
    Author clean, consistent JSON variable files and apply baseline naming/tagging conventions.
    Maintain an “outputs journal” so you can accurately reuse IDs/OCIDs across modules.
    Validate plans/applies, interpret common errors, and verify that resources land in the correct compartments with the expected tags and network reachability.
    Clean up in the right order (networking before IAM/compartments) to avoid dependency issues and stray costs.
     

By the end, you will have a minimal Landing Zone composed of a compartment structure with baseline policies, one VCN with public/private subnets and essential gateways/route tables/NSGs, and a tag namespace with defined tags applied to resources. The result is not production-ready; it is a clear, reproducible demonstration of the modular approach that prepares you to scale up and later adopt the Landing Zone Orchestrator. If you elect to use OpenTofu or other third-party tooling, ensure alignment with Oracle’s internal security and compliance guidelines. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Enable two users—one with elevated privileges and one with limited access—to query banking data using natural language and vector-based recommendations, while enforcing strict access controls. In this hands-on workshop, participants will build an "AI-Powered Banking Insights Application" using Oracle 23ai Autonomous Database (ADB) and Oracle Application Express (APEX), secured with Virtual Private Database (VPD) policies to enforce fine-grained access control. The application enables two user types—a privileged user (bank_manager) with full access to sensitive customer and loan data, and a restricted user (bank_staff) limited to public service data—to interact with banking insights via natural language queries (e.g., "Show me customers with credit scores above 700") and AI-driven vector search for personalised recommendations.
Key features include:
Database Setup: Create tables under the admin schema, with vector columns.
AI Integration: Configure AI PROFILE using DBMS_CLOUD_AI for natural language processing and with an in-database ONNX model for vector embeddings, enabling Select AI functionality.
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Implement secure access
VPD Security: Use VPD policies to enforce row-level security, ensuring unauthorised users cannot access sensitive data.
APEX Application: Develop an APEX application supporting database authentication for manager and staff.
The application includes:
Banking Insights Dashboard (for bank_manager): Query sensitive data with natural language (e.g., credit scores, loan eligibility).
Service Queries Page (for both users): Access service-related data with restricted access for bank_staff.
Recommendations Page (for bank_manager): Provide AI-driven loan recommendations using vector search. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Discover how graph technology turns security data into attack maps. Using Oracle Graph and Linkurious Ogma, security teams can connect logs, users, devices, and events to uncover hidden relationships, trace attack paths, spot suspicious patterns, and accelerate threat hunting and incident response. Modern cyberattacks rarely consist of a single suspicious event. Instead, they unfold through a sequence of interconnected actions involving users, systems, devices, network connections, and applications. Understanding these relationships is essential for detecting threats, investigating incidents, and responding effectively. In this session, we demonstrate how graph technology can transform complex security data—such as network logs, authentication records, and security events—into an intuitive graph model that reveals attack paths, hidden relationships, and suspicious patterns. By representing entities as nodes and interactions as edges, investigators can move beyond isolated alerts and gain a complete view of an attack's progression. Using Oracle Graph for in-database graph queries, pattern matching, and graph analytics, together with Linkurious' high-performance Ogma visualization technology, we show how security teams can explore large-scale attack scenarios, identify critical connections, and accelerate threat investigations. Through practical demonstrations, attendees will learn how graph analytics and visualization work together to support cyber threat hunting and incident response.

But starting in Oracle Database 23ai, it’s now possible to track positions within spatiotemporal dimensions, so it’s now possible to build sophisticated logistics and position tracking applications on a grand scale. Oracle 23ai’s advanced spatio-temporal features offer the ability to not only identify exactly where a point on the surface of the earth is and what geography it lies within, but now also when a particular object has entered, remained within, and finally left the confines of a specific geospatial boundary. 
We’ll show how these new abilities make it possible to build sophisticated logistics and tracking geospatial applications at scale using a real-world example: identifying which electric vehicles (EVs) are approaching, currently using, just leaving, or circling a large-scale EV charging station.
This session will:
- Explain Oracle Database 23ai spatio-temporal features
- Explore the potential logistics and tracking capabilities now made possible through this feature set
- Demonstrate how these features can be leveraged within a sample APEX application not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

This hands-on lab walks you through configuring network isolation, setting up a private LLM host, and enabling Select AI to safely query data. By the end, you’ll know how to combine LLM power with Oracle’s enterprise-grade security. In this hands-on workshop, you will learn how to securely integrate large language models (LLMs) with Oracle Autonomous Database Select AI by leveraging private endpoints. Private endpoints provide network isolation and ensure that communication between your Autonomous Database and AI models does not traverse the public internet, meeting strict enterprise security and compliance requirements.

The lab guides you step-by-step through creating a Virtual Cloud Network (VCN), configuring private endpoints, and deploying a jump server and private LLM host. You will then provision an Autonomous Database instance with Private Endpoint access, install and configure an Ollama AI model, and use it with Select AI for secure natural language prompting.

records.title: Configure Hub-and-Spoke Routing for an Active/Passive Palo Alto NGFW Deployment in OCI
records.rawTitle: Configure Hub-and-Spoke Routing for an Active/Passive Palo Alto NGFW Deployment in OCI
records.source: 28 September 2026 WMS, dashboard views, and WMS tag reports; GitHub repository/update evidence retained from 14-15 August 2026
details: Learn how to steer traffic through an Active/Passive Palo Alto Networks VM-Series HA pair in an OCI Hub-and-Spoke topology. This workshop covers the same nine North-South and East-West routing scenarios as the standalone workshop, but routes every flow to the floating secondary IP addresses so that traffic follows the active firewall automatically after a failover.

An Active/Passive Palo Alto Networks VM-Series HA pair changes one thing about Hub-and-Spoke routing in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and it changes it everywhere: the route target. OCI route rules cannot point at "whichever firewall is active" — they point at a private IP. In an Active/Passive design that IP is a secondary (floating) IP address on the data VNICs, which PAN-OS moves from the failed member to the surviving member during a failover. Every route rule in the topology must target that floating IP rather than a primary interface IP, or the design will survive a lab test and break during a real failover.

This workshop is the Active/Passive variant of the final part of the Palo Alto Networks in OCI series. The earlier parts covered deploying the HA pair itself, including the HA1 control link, the HA2 data link, the floating secondary IPs, and the IAM policy that allows the firewall to move those IPs between instances. This part shifts the focus to routing and end-to-end connectivity around that pair.

You will work through nine routing scenarios, each with its own use case, traffic flow, OCI route table configuration, matching PAN-OS virtual router configuration, and a validation step.

North-South scenarios cover a public Application Load Balancer with a WAF policy placed in front of the HA pair; the HA pair placed in front of a private Application Load Balancer with destination NAT; centralized outbound Internet access for spoke workloads with source NAT; and remote user access through GlobalProtect VPN with split-tunnel routing.

East-West scenarios cover a centralized Service Gateway in the hub with full firewall inspection of Oracle Services Network traffic; distributed Service Gateways in each spoke that bypass inspection; subnet-to-subnet traffic inside a single spoke VCN forced through the firewall; spoke-to-spoke traffic between two VCNs routed through the firewall; and hybrid connectivity over an IPSec VPN between the HA pair in one OCI region and an OCI native Dynamic Routing Gateway in another.

Each scenario adds a failover validation step. You will confirm that the session survives, or fails and re-establishes as designed, when the active member is taken out of service, and you will inspect the session table on the newly active member to prove that state synchronization over the HA2 link is doing its job.

Along the way you will apply the Hub-and-Spoke design guidelines that make these topologies predictable and debuggable: a dedicated hub VCN for shared services, one subnet per firewall interface including the dedicated HA subnet, per-spoke DRG attachments with DRG route tables, DRG import route distributions so the hub learns spoke CIDRs dynamically, and DRG attachment ingress route tables that keep return traffic symmetric.

Get Started with Oracle Query Service 12014 OCI lauran.serhal@oracle.com Workshop Approved oci Mapped From Current Wms 12014 Workshop Approved OCI 2/5/2026 3/1/2026 Individual author Individual oci Mapped From Current Wms github_pages Live GitHub repository-level proxy (high confidence) high Repository-level Git proxy 2026-08-14 2026-08-14 2026-08-14 Add Palo Alto Site-to-Site IPSec VPN (P4) and GlobalProtect VPN (P5) … anabdall Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 12014 Workshop Approved OCI 2/5/2026 3/1/2026 Individual author Individual https://oracle-livelabs.github.io/oci/query-service/get-started/workshops/tenancy/index.html lauran.serhal@oracle.com DB Product Management Oracle Query Service makes it easy to run secure Oracle SQL queries across sources like OCI Object Storage and Delta Sharing tables. There’s no database setup or maintenance required—just start querying. Pay only for the compute you use. Access the service through the OCI Console, APIs, or Oracle client tools. Oracle Query Service is an OCI native, serverless platform for running Oracle SQL across multiple data sources—no database provisioning or management required. 

Projects, the service's core organizational unit, group related tables, views, worksheets, and queries. Each project can access various sources: 

 

OCI Object Storage (with direct querying) 

Delta Sharing providers (for interoperable data sharing and synchronization) 

Pre-defined public datasets 

You can also create tables from query results or ingest data from public HTTP/HTTPS endpoints. 

 

Submit queries using three main interfaces: 

 

OCI Console UI (with graphical query builder and worksheets) 

REST and SDK APIs 

Direct SQL client connections (JDBC, SQL Developer, SQL*Net) 

 

Worksheets help manage multiple queries but are UI-only—they can't be accessed via APIs. All queries are billed per Enterprise Compute (ECPU) resources used, with compute provisioned on demand. No persistent database is linked to any project. 

 

Query results land in a staging area and are kept for three days by default. You can export results to your OCI Object Storage or materialize them as new project tables. Pagination for results is available through all interfaces. Security relies on OCI Identity and Access Management (IAM), with permissions at project and query execution levels, plus network access controls for direct connections. 

 

Delta Sharing lets you list, update, and delete providers, browse shared tables, and synchronize data either on demand or by schedule. Synchronized tables become native within the project, available for queries and views. 

 

Oracle Query Service supports full Oracle SQL syntax and semantics, working seamlessly with Oracle Database tools and APIs. It fits teams needing flexible, secure analytics across diverse data sources. Typical uses: 

 

Exploring large datasets in object storage 

Federated querying via Delta Sharing 

Prototyping and experimentation 

Operational analytics without the cost of dedicated databases 

 

With Oracle Query Service, organizations can simplify data exploration, processing, and delivery—while preserving security, governance, and cost efficiency. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Learn how to maximize use of APEX Interactive Grids to meet most any data presentation and edit requirement and keep you end users happy across your enterprise.  This workshop will teach you how to leverage interactive grid declarative and customization features to meet all of your business needs, then walk you through steps  to standardize your settings and customization to minimize coding effort, maximize efficiency and ensure consistency across all interactive grids in all your applications.  

You will generate an APEX application that includes an interactive grid. You will learn to customize column settings, declaratively and by code, to control what users are able to do (or not) with each column. You explore declarative toolbar configuration settings.  You will next define and implement several custom grid view toolbar and action menu configurations.  You will explore the interaction of declarative and custom toolbar configuration settings. Oracle GoldenGate Extract does not support seamless role transitioning from a primary to a secondary Extract with PostgreSQL high availability configurations. However, manual procedural operations could be followed to provide continuity from the new primary Extract.
In this Lab we are running a solution to avoid the manual operation and instead use pg_dump and pg_restore utilities with LSN based backup which would avoid the unneccessary use of deploying extra EXTRACT and REPLICAT for doing the initial load. details: Turn an inventory upload into instant insights. Deploy Python with OCI Functions’ code-only capability and automate processing with OCI Events.

Build an event-driven inventory-processing workflow with Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Functions. In this beginner-friendly workshop, you deploy Python code using the code-only Functions capability, without building or pushing a container image.

Starting with a prepared environment, you explore how Functions applications, functions, and events work together. Review a tested Python implementation—or use a supplied prompt with an AI coding assistant—then validate the processing logic in OCI Cloud Shell. Deploy the function from a ZIP archive and configure OCI Events to invoke it whenever a CSV file is uploaded to an Object Storage bucket.

Your function processes the inventory file and writes two reports: products below a configurable stock threshold and records that need correction. Upload sample data and verify the results to see the complete workflow in action.

Optional exercises show how to change the restocking threshold without modifying code and use invocation logs to investigate an invalid record. Leave with a practical understanding of serverless deployment, event-driven automation, configuration, and troubleshooting on OCI.

GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback External Or Legacy Url Unmapped Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 4481 Workshop In Development Database 9/8/2025 3/1/2021 Individual author Individual https://oracle.github.io/learning-library/data-management-library/database-consolidation/workshop/ tejus.subrahmanya@oracle.com NA Cloud SE Oracle Databases consolidation workshop Database consolidation involves placing multiple databases onto a single set of computing infrastructure, either on-premise or in the Oracle Cloud. Database consolidation is different from server consolidation, which involves consolidating multiple physical servers into a single physical server running Virtual Machines. The primary purpose of database consolidation is to reduce the cost of database infrastructure by taking advantage of more powerful servers that have come onto the market that include dozens of processor cores in a single server.

Databases consolidation may involve any of the following configurations:
Multiple databases on a single physical server
Multiple databases on a single virtual machine
Multiple databases on a cluster of physical servers
Multiple databases on a cluster of virtual machines

Database consolidation allows more databases to run on fewer servers, which reduces infrastructure, but also reduces operational costs. Each physical server represents an Information Technology asset or “Configuration Item” (CI) that must be placed into a data center rack, connected, secured, and maintained. Each Virtual Machine represents another Configuration Item (CI) that also must be deployed, connected (virtually), secured, and maintained.  Database consolidation can significantly reduce the number of CI’s that need to be managed, thereby reducing operational expenses.
 
Database Consolidation also applies in Cloud environments such as the Oracle Database Cloud Service and Oracle Exadata Cloud Service. Oracle databases can also be consolidated into a cluster of physical servers or virtual machines. Oracle Database clustering capabilities include active/passive clustering, as well as active/active clustering using Oracle Real Application Clusters. Clustering is used to increase availability of Oracle databases, enable rolling patching, and to provide for scalability across multiple physical servers or virtual machines.
 
Oracle databases can also be further consolidated into what are known as Container Databases using the Oracle Multitenant option that was first introduced in Oracle Database 12c. The Multitenant option allows multiple databases to be managed under a single Container Database, with a single backup, single disaster recovery configuration, and single clustering configuration. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.

Building Your First CICD Project On OCI with ADB 11759 OCI ashu.kumar@oracle.com Workshop Approved pts Mapped From Current Wms 11759 Workshop Approved OCI 10/4/2024 12/20/2024 Individual author Individual pts Mapped From Current Wms github_repo Local Git mirror repository-level proxy (high confidence) high Repository-level Git proxy 2026-03-12 2026-03-12 Update copyright current year Lucian Brinzei Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 11759 Workshop Approved OCI 10/4/2024 12/20/2024 Individual author Individual https://github.com/oracle-livelabs/pts/tree/main/cicd/ ashu.kumar@oracle.com DB Product Management Learn to build CICD Project On OCI from the ground up. This hands-on workshop covers project creation, code repository setup, Kubernetes cluster deployment, Autonomous Database configuration, build and deploy pipelines, and accessing your application. Follow step-by-step instructions to set up an OKE cluster, create a build pipeline, and deploy a sample Todo App with live monitoring. Join our in-depth workshop to master creating CICD Project On OCI from scratch. This session will guide you through each essential step:

1. Create a Project: Start by setting up a new OCI project through the OCI console.
   
2. Set Up Code Repository: Configure your code repository and download the Todo App code sample.

3. Deploy Kubernetes Cluster: Use the wizard to create an Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE) cluster with default settings.

4. Create an Autonomous Database: Set up an Autonomous Database with default configurations. Download and replace the wallet, upload sample data, and update the configuration file.

5. Build Pipeline Creation: 
   - Name your Build Pipeline.
   - Add stages to create and push Docker images and Kubernetes manifests.
   - Configure artifacts for Docker images and Kubernetes manifests, linking them to build results.

6. Environment Setup: Define an Oracle Kubernetes Engine environment for use in the deploy pipeline.

7. Deploy Pipeline Creation:
   - Name your Deploy Pipeline.
   - Add a stage to apply Kubernetes manifests.
   - Configure the pipeline to use the previously created OKE environment and cluster.

8. Trigger Deployment: Link your Build Pipeline to the Deploy Pipeline to automate deployment triggers.

9. Run and Monitor: Execute the Build Pipeline manually, monitor both the build and deploy processes to ensure successful execution.

10. Access the Application:
    - Retrieve your application’s URL from the OKE cluster details.
    - Use Cloud Shell to access and monitor Kubernetes resources.
    - Copy the LoadBalancer’s External IP, append port 5000, and browse to view your deployed Todo App.

The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an open, vendor-neutral, industry standard application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services over an Internet Protocol (IP) network. details: Learn how to set up your database instance as an AI Proxy Database to access remote data for use with Select AI. without having to move your data to Oracle.

Customers store data in a variety of sources and may be unable to migrate their data to Oracle, but that’s not a problem for Select AI. Using what we refer to as an AI Proxy Database approach, also known as a “sidecar,” you can extend Select AI beyond your database by exposing external data sources as objects in your database schema. If Select AI can “see” such tables or views, it can leverage your chosen LLM to generate federated SQL queries across them. Remote data sources can be both Oracle and non-Oracle data sources, whether in the cloud or on premises.

In this workshop, you'll map sources into your database schema, creating views over database links and define external tables. You can even add local table and column comments or annotations to improve intent and accuracy.

The AI Proxy Database approach can be used on both Oracle AI Database and Autonomous AI Database 26ai and 19c.

OCI Open LZ - Configure your Tailored Landing Zone 11489 OCI paola.juarez@oracle.com Workshop Approved No Repository Url 11489 Workshop Approved OCI 10/23/2023 11/30/2023 Individual author Individual No Repository Url No repository URL is present in the current WMS export. GitHub repository not mapped; WMS record timestamp fallback (unknown confidence) unknown WMS metadata fallback No Repository Url Pending Livelabs Identity No LiveLabs ID or Publish Type exists in the current WMS row. 11489 Workshop Approved OCI 10/23/2023 11/30/2023 Individual author Individual paola.juarez@oracle.com EMEA Domain Specialists The OCI Open LZ simplifies the onboarding of organizations, business units, and subsidiaries into OCI. It is a reference blueprint and a repeatable design process of an end-to-end solution.  With this LiveLab you will setup the OCI Open LZ through simple IaC configurations, with human-readable JSON/HCLs, giving you the ability to master the approach to create and tailor your own landing zones. Welcome to the OCI Open LZ  LiveLab, a guided process to create and run the OCI Open LZ blueprint in your own tenancy, and scale your abilities to setup and run any OCI resource topology. The main benefits are:

Focus on Value: Focus on configuring the design and resources, instead of coding them. This means shorter time-to-value, lower effort, and lower risk.  
Best Practices: Use existing top-quality terraform modules that are open and full of best practices. It's possible to leverage this to evolve OCI terraform skills and apply future IaC best practices. This also means lower risk and lower efforts.
Scale Day Two: Being able to split operational configurations from code is a game change in cloud operations, and will simplify drastically the day-two operations, opening the path for a GitOps operating model and potentially simpler automation. The cloud operators will only work with configurations, not code.


With this LiveLabs you will be able to setup and run the OCI Open LZ or any tailored landing zone normally used in these use cases (but not limited to):

Mirroring existing landing zones on other CSPs.
Onboarding and reflecting organization structures such as business units, operating entities, OpCos, into a cloud operating model.
Fine-grained segregation of duties and responsibilities across resources and teams.
Network structure with different areas and security postures, with fine-tuned north-south and east-west traffic scenarios.
Heterogeneous and/or large workloads landscape.
Adopting a highly scalable operating model, such as control versioned operations.


The OCI Open LZ use the configurable Terraform CIS Landing Zone Enhanced Modules (IAM, Networking, Security, and Observability & Monitoring), a collection of repositories created to help customers align and configure their OCI implementations with the CIS OCI Foundations Benchmark recommendations. These modules work under the same approach:

Allow the definition of arbitrary resource topologies in a JSON/HCL format.
Enforce CIS Benchmark recommendations when appropriate.
Require minimal Terraform knowledge to be utilised.

With the OCI Open LZ configurable approach used on this LiveLabs you be able to avoid the common pitfalls, such as:

Hard-coding. Changing or adapting code to create a new landing zone different than an existing solution is complex and time-consuming. This also means that any change to the landing zone will be executed by code and not configurations.
Waste & Late Time-to-Value. The time spent on adapting code, or re-coding over and over for the OCI landing/core resources is time wasted and not used on the business value/workloads.
Limited Scaling. Doing OCI changes manually can work for some tactical solutions, but it will always limit the scaling and add complexity and cost to the day-two operations. Note that, for example, CIS LZ creates 100+ OCI resources.
Scarce Skills. IaC Terraform coding skills are not as common as we should expect, which makes these efforts a higher risk and challenge to solve. not_in_dashboard_snapshot unavailable No exact title row exists in the 28 September 2026 dashboard workbook.
